14	CASE OD2-DEV-OBVWRONG (OBVWRONG, organizational): Larkmoor Parks: the maintenance overtime overrun
15	Setting: The Larkmoor Parks and Open Space Department (fictional) maintains parks in four districts: Riverside, Eastgate, Millbrook and Summit Hill. The maintenance division has 112 maintenance-worker positions. This year the city adopted several budget reductions, including a citywide hiring freeze from 6 January. Maintenance overtime for April–September is well over budget, and the council's Finance Committee wants an explanation and a corrective plan.
16	Presenting request: The Budget Office has asked you to explain the overtime overrun in the parks maintenance division and recommend what the department should do before the Finance Committee deadline of 15 December. The Director believes the hiring freeze is the cause and has asked for an exemption to fill eleven positions.
17	INITIAL EVIDENCE
18	E1 [stage S1] Office of Budget & Management memo to the Parks Director (financial-record): Re: Overtime variance, April–September. Parks maintenance overtime for April–September totals $688,400, compared with $412,100 for the same months last year (+67%) and a budget of $430,000. Council's Finance Committee has asked for an explanation and corrective plan by 15 December. For reference, this year's adopted reductions for the department were: citywide hiring freeze on non-public-safety positions (from 6 January); deferral of two mower replacements ($118,000); non-renewal of the after-hours closing services contract ($96,000); reduced seasonal temp hours ($40,000). Please route your response through this office.
19	E2 [stage S1] Interview notes, Director Ruth Okafor-Lind, 3 November (leadership-account): 'This is the hiring freeze, plain and simple. We started the year six maintenance workers short and we're at seventeen now. Every vacancy is a route somebody has to cover after their shift. July was brutal too, because the heat meant extra irrigation checks and mowing catch-up. I've asked the City Manager for an exemption to fill eleven positions; that brings overtime back to normal within a quarter.' Asked about other drivers, she said the closing contract 'was a small line, crews absorbed it.' She said she had not seen a breakdown of overtime by pay code.
20	E3 [stage S1] HR/payroll extract prepared at the Director's request (system-record): Maintenance division, current year. Month: vacant maintenance-worker positions (of 112) / overtime paid. Jan 6 / $52.3k; Feb 8 / $49.1k; Mar 10 / $55.0k; Apr 12 / $104.2k; May 15 / $109.0k; Jun 17 / $118.1k; Jul 17 / $121.4k; Aug 17 / $119.3k; Sep 17 / $116.4k. HR analyst note: correlation between monthly vacancies and monthly overtime, January–September, r = 0.93. 'Overtime has tracked the vacancy count closely all year.'
21	E4 [stage S1] Interview notes, Dale Visconti, crew lead, Millbrook district, 5 November (staff-account): 'We're running routes two and three people short. Guys are holding over an hour or two most days to finish mowing. On top of that, since spring we're back out at night a few times a week, and nobody's seen their kids in months. Morale is the lowest I've seen in nineteen years. If they'd just fill the positions this would sort itself out.' He estimated he personally had worked 'about 25 hours of overtime a month' since April.
22	E5 [stage S1] City Ethics Hotline intake record #2611 (log): Received 22 August from an anonymous caller identifying as a parks employee. Allegation: two Riverside maintenance workers (named in the sealed record as Employees R-14 and R-22) 'are claiming night call-backs for parks they never go to. It's all paper slips, nobody checks. They're each pulling an extra grand a month.' Caller declined follow-up contact. Status: referred to Internal Audit for review on 26 August.
23	E6 [stage S1] Email from the Municipal Employees Local 418 steward to the Director, 7 November (staff-account): Members are exhausted and grievances are coming. Two points. First, in Eastgate the night lock-ups keep going to the same handful of people the supervisor likes, and others never get asked. Second, if management answers this with an overtime cap, understand that members will stop taking call-backs, and then the gates and restrooms don't get locked. Nobody wants a repeat of the splash-pad break-in two years ago. Fill the vacancies and treat people fairly.
24	E7 [stage S1] Risk Management quarterly summary, parks maintenance (system-record): Workers' compensation claims filed April–September: 15 (prior year, same period: 9). Claim types: strains/sprains 8, lacerations 3, slips/falls 3, other 1. Lost workdays: 112 (prior: 61). Safety coordinator's note: 'The rise coincides with heavy overtime; fatigue is a likely factor and we recommend a review.' No analysis of hours worked by individual claimants has been performed.
25	CATALOGUE (full contents)
26	C1 [stage S1] City Manager hiring-freeze directive and citywide exemption log - City Manager's Office (document): Directive 2026-01 freezes all non-public-safety hiring from 6 January until further notice. Departments may request exemptions for positions 'essential to health, safety, or legally mandated service.' Exemption log to date: 9 requests citywide, 4 approved (all in the water utility and 911 dispatch). Parks submitted one request on 28 October for 11 maintenance-worker positions; it is pending. The directive does not restrict overtime or contract spending.
27	C2 [stage S1] Regional weather station summary, April–September, current and prior year - Larkmoor airport weather station (external-data): Days at or above 35°C: 6 (prior year 2). Mean July high 31.8°C (prior 30.1°C). April–September rainfall 388 mm (prior 402 mm). Growing-season degree days +4%. All four parks districts lie within 9 km of the station; no district-level variation is recorded.
28	C3 [stage S1] Budget office overtime workbook by pay code and district, April–September, current and prior year - Office of Budget & Management, payroll analytics (financial-record): April–September, prior year → current year. By pay code: OT-X holdover $341.0k → $358.1k (hours +1.5%; rest reflects the 3.5% July wage increase); CB call-back $38.2k → $289.3k; other (holiday, storm, event) $32.9k → $41.0k. By district: total OT, call-back portion, and vacant positions at 30 September. Riverside $112k → $205k, CB $10k → $95k, 5 of 30 vacant. Eastgate $104k → $200k, CB $9k → $98k, 1 of 30 vacant. Millbrook $98k → $179k, CB $9k → $84k, 6 of 28 vacant. Summit Hill $98k → $104k, CB $10k → $12k, 5 of 24 vacant. Call-back entries: 2,295 (prior 312); 1,962 carry task code CLOSE (prior 0), all dated 1 April or later, none in Summit Hill; other call-backs 333. Data aggregated by district; no employee-level detail.
29	C4 [stage S1] Workers' compensation claim log, parks maintenance, April–September - Risk Management claims system (system-record): Fifteen claims. Each entry lists date, time of injury, task and injury type; the district field is blank on most entries. 11 of 15 injuries occurred between 07:00 and 13:00; 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting. The claim form does not record hours worked in the preceding 24 hours or whether the employee had worked a call-back the previous night, and payroll records have not been matched to claims. The prior-year log shows a similar task mix (6 of 9 involved mowing, trimming or lifting).
30	C5 [stage S1] Collective agreement excerpts, Articles 12 and 14 (overtime and call-back) - City–Local 418 collective agreement (document): Art. 12.3: work beyond the scheduled 8-hour shift is paid at 1.5× in 15-minute increments. Art. 12.7: management may not change regular shift start times without 30 days' notice and consultation. Art. 14.1: an employee recalled to work after leaving the worksite receives a minimum of three hours' pay at 1.5×, regardless of time worked. Art. 14.4: call-back is voluntary unless no volunteer is available, in which case the least-senior qualified employee is directed. Wage schedule: 3.5% increase effective 1 July.
31	C6 [stage S1] Procurement file for the after-hours closing services contract, with related operational memo - Purchasing Division file PK-2219; Deputy Director memo of 24 March (change-record): Contract PK-2219 with Kestrel Night Services covered nightly closing of gates, restrooms and splash pads at 41 sites in Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook for $96,000 a year. It expired 31 March and was not renewed (adopted budget reduction). Summit Hill's 12 sites are closed under a separate contract paid by the Summit Hill Business Improvement District, which continued unchanged. Memo, Deputy Director Paul Senanayake, 24 March: 'From 1 April, nightly closing at the 41 sites will be done by maintenance staff on call-back under Art. 14. Supervisors will post sign-up sheets. Closing is a condition of the city's liability coverage and must not be skipped.' Margin note: 'Net saving est. $60k after modest OT.'
32	C7 [stage S1] HR exit interview summaries, maintenance workers separating January–September - Human Resources (document): Eleven separations (8 resignations, 3 retirements). Primary reasons cited by those who resigned: higher pay elsewhere (5), commute or relocation (2), conflict with a supervisor (1). Three mentioned 'too much overtime' as a secondary reason. Under the hiring freeze, no position was backfilled.
33	C8 [stage S1] Interview with the Eastgate district supervisor - Interview notes, Marisol Adeyemi-Clark, Eastgate supervisor, 10 November (manager-account): 'I post a sign-up sheet every Monday for the week's closings. The same five or six people sign up most nights, because others have childcare or second jobs. If nobody signs, I direct the junior person, like the contract says. I don't keep the old sheets; they go in the bin when the week's over.' She said no one had told her about a complaint. She declined to estimate how call-backs were split among her 29 staff.
34	C9 [stage S1] Internal Audit memo on hotline intake #2611 - Internal Audit memo IA-26-31, 30 October (prior-report): Auditors matched 120 call-back claims (April–August) against electronic gate-controller and restroom smart-lock event logs, including all 64 claims by Employees R-14 and R-22. For 117 of 120 claims (and 64 of 64 for R-14 and R-22), the logs show lock events at the claimed sites within 40 minutes of the claimed time. The three exceptions were at sites without smart locks, and supervisor sign-off sheets confirm attendance. Conclusion: no evidence of claims for work not performed. Observation: under the 3-hour minimum, each 30–45 minute closing round is paid as three hours.
35	C10 [stage S1] Recreation division event permit summary, April–September - Recreation permit system (system-record): Athletic field and pavilion permits issued: 1,284 (prior year 1,236, +4%). Events requiring staff attendance after 18:00: 61 (prior 58). Tournament weekends: 14 (prior 13). Event staffing overtime is charged to the Recreation cost center under pay code EV, not to the maintenance division.
36	C11 [stage S1] Fleet maintenance log for parks mowers and utility vehicles, January–September - City Fleet Services (log): Both mowers whose replacement was deferred remained in service. Unplanned mower downtime: 47 unit-days (prior year 39). Longest outage: 9 days (Riverside, June). On 6 occasions, work orders note that crews 'doubled up on remaining units.' No vehicle downtime affecting evening or night operations was recorded.
37	C12 [stage S1] Regional parks benchmarking survey: overtime share of maintenance payroll, prior fiscal year - Regional municipal parks association (external-data): Eight comparable municipalities. Overtime as a share of maintenance payroll: median 7.2%, range 4.1%–11.8%. Larkmoor, prior year: 6.9%. Figures are self-reported and the survey does not break out pay codes. Current-year figures have not yet been collected.
38	CANDIDATES
39	H1: The overtime increase is driven mainly by maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze, with crews working extra hours to cover open routes.
40	H2: The overtime increase is driven mainly by nightly closing duties moved onto maintenance staff as 3-hour-minimum call-backs after the after-hours closing contract was not renewed.
41	H3: Padded or fictitious call-back claims account for a material share of the overtime increase.
42	H4: Extra irrigation and mowing work caused by the hot summer is a main driver of the overtime increase.
43	H5: In Eastgate, the supervisor is steering lock-up call-backs to a favored subset of staff.
44	R1: Rise in maintenance vacancies under the hiring freeze -> Rise in maintenance overtime spending, April–September (causes)
45	R2: Non-renewal of the after-hours closing contract for Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook -> Rise in call-back overtime in those three districts (causes)
46	R3: Higher overtime hours among maintenance staff -> Rise in workers' compensation injury claims (causes)
47	A1: Restore contracted nightly closing for the 41 Riverside, Eastgate and Millbrook sites (through an emergency extension or a re-tender, mirroring the Summit Hill arrangement), and track call-back spending against the April–September level.
48	A2: Impose an immediate department-wide cap of 12 overtime hours per worker per month.
49	A3: Refer Employees R-14 and R-22 for disciplinary investigation and suspend their call-back eligibility in the meantime.
50	A4: Remove the Eastgate supervisor from call-back scheduling and issue her a written reprimand for favoritism.
51	SCORED ITEMS
52	IT-H1: hypothesis H1 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
53	IT-H2: hypothesis H2 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
54	IT-H3: hypothesis H3 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
55	IT-H4: hypothesis H4 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
56	IT-H5: hypothesis H5 allowed=[supported, contradicted, unknown]
57	IT-R1: edge R1 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
58	IT-R2: edge R2 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
59	IT-R3: edge R3 allowed=[causal, association-only, contradicted, unknown]
60	IT-A1: action A1 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
61	IT-A2: action A2 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
62	IT-A3: action A3 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
63	IT-A4: action A4 allowed=[preferred, acceptable, premature, harmful]
64	IT-SUFF: sufficiency SUFF allowed=[sufficient, insufficient]

answers.justification: Of the +$276k increase, about $251k is call-back pay (C3). Holdover hours rose only 1.5% (C3). Summit Hill has 5 vacancies but flat overtime, while Eastgate has 1 vacancy and doubled overtime (C3). So the r=0.93 in E3 reflects the April step change, not vacancy coverage.

From 1 April, closing at the 41 sites moved to Art. 14 call-backs with a 3-hour minimum (C6, C5, C9). There are 1,962 CLOSE call-backs, none in Summit Hill, and call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k (C3). Summit Hill kept its separate contract and its overtime stayed flat (C6, C3).

Internal Audit matched all 64 claims by R-14 and R-22, and 117 of 120 sampled claims, to lock event logs. The other 3 were confirmed by sign-off sheets, so no fictitious claims were found (C9). The extra pay is explained by the 3-hour minimum.

The weather was only modestly hotter (C2). Holdover hours, where extra mowing or irrigation work would show up, rose only 1.5% (C3). Summit Hill shares the same weather but its overtime was flat (C2, C3).

The steward's favoritism claim (E6) has an equally plausible innocent explanation: sign-up is voluntary and childcare limits who signs up (C8, C5). The sign-up sheets are thrown away and there is no employee-level data (C8, C3), so the evidence cannot tell these apart.

Vacancies and overtime move together (E3), but holdover hours were nearly flat (C3). Districts with more vacancies did not show more overtime growth: Summit Hill and Eastgate contradict it (C3). The April jump matches the end of the contract, not the vacancy trend (C6).

The CLOSE call-backs start exactly on 1 April (C3). The memo directs closing to be done by call-back (C6), and the 3-hour minimum provides the mechanism (C5). Summit Hill, whose contract continued, is a control district with no rise (C3, C6).
In aggregate, claims rose while overtime rose (E7). However, claims were never matched to hours worked, and the timing and task mix match the prior year (C4). Causation is therefore not established.

The contract cost $96k a year (C6), while closing call-backs added about $250k in six months (C3). Closing is required for liability coverage (C6), and the Summit Hill arrangement shows the model works.

A cap would not address the call-back mechanism (C3, C5). The union warns members would stop taking call-backs (E6), which risks leaving sites unclosed even though closing is a condition of liability coverage (C6).
The audit verified every claim by R-14 and R-22 against lock logs (C9). Disciplining them would punish employees who have already been cleared.

Favoritism has not been established. The supervisor's practice of posting voluntary sign-ups and directing the junior person when no one signs follows Art. 14.4 (C8, C5), and the only allegation is the steward's (E6).

The pay-code and district breakdown (C3), the contract and memo (C6), the Summit Hill control district, and the audit (C9) together identify the driver clearly enough to justify restoring the closing contract.

IT-A4: 'harmful' is also defensible, because a written reprimand without evidence of favoritism risks punishing the wrong party.
caseProblems: The arithmetic is internally consistent across E1, E3, C3, C7 and C8: month totals, pay-code and district totals, vacancy counts, and the 29 Eastgate staff all check out. No leakage through catalogue titles was found.
Minor: the case does not say whether R3's 'higher overtime hours' means paid hours or worked hours. Under the 3-hour minimum these differ substantially, which makes IT-R3 harder to answer.
